summary: The paper analyzes quantum algorithms for financial risk measurement (Value‑at‑Risk and Potential Future Exposure) using Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation. Small simulator experiments with 2–3 qubits per risk factor show discretization errors of ~14% for VaR and ~5–10% for PFE quantiles, while realistic noise levels (~0.1% gate error) can introduce >25% estimation errors, leading the authors to conclude that practical applications require orders‑of‑magnitude more qubits than current devices.

experiments.description: Market risk (VaR) experiment using a two-risk-factor Monte Carlo-style quantum circuit with empirical marginal distributions loaded via piecewise transformations and Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation on a simulator.

algorithm.variant: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) for VaR

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Two correlated risk-factor return distributions are loaded into quantum registers; each marginal is discretized with q qubits and transformed from normal to empirical returns via piecewise linear/cubic functions. A comparator marks whether normalized P&L is below a threshold for CDF estimation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the CDF of normalized portfolio P&L and derive VaR quantiles from it.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Comparator-based thresholding for CDF estimation; no QUBO/penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: Two-asset market risk portfolio based on Microsoft (msft) and Apple (aapl) ten-day returns; portfolio P&L approximated by first-order sensitivities.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: 10-day overlapping log-returns; standardized by mean and standard deviation; empirical CDF fit with piecewise cubic or piecewise linear functions

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Daily closing prices converted to 10-day overlapping log-returns; mean drift set to zero; returns standardized; empirical CDFs fitted to normal quantiles; correlated normal distribution calibrated with covariance matrix from historical data.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Quantum simulator results compared against classical continuous and discretized Monte Carlo-style reference distributions; VaR quantiles reported at 1%, 2.5%, and 5%.

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical Monte Carlo / continuous reference distribution
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Historical calibration of marginal distributions and covariance; piecewise fitting of empirical CDFs; classical computation of reference VaR values.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Bisection search over the CDF to obtain VaR quantiles; relative unsigned error computed against classical reference.

speedup_claims.conditions: QAE / IQAE estimation of expected values and CDFs
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states the original QAE has O(M^-1) convergence versus O(M^-1/2) for classical Monte Carlo; practical circuits are large and noisy.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) convergence for QAE estimation error; quadratic improvement over Monte Carlo

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not estimated; authors state real applications would require orders of magnitude more qubits than current ~100-qubit devices
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Thousands to millions of qubits to represent realistic portfolios with thousands of risk factors
limiting_factors: Very limited number of qubits for representing many risk factors
Distribution loading and arithmetic circuits require large ancilla overhead
Discretization error with small q (2–3 qubits per factor)
Quantum noise not included in main VaR experiment
Classical Monte Carlo already fast enough in practice

notes: The paper states all computations are carried out on a quantum simulator using Qiskit, but does not name a specific simulator backend.

The exact total qubit count for the full market-risk circuit is not stated explicitly in one place; the paper reports q=2 or q=3 qubits per risk factor plus additional ancillas, so total num_qubits is left null rather than guessed.
Authors explicitly state the business case for quantum solutions is currently weak.
Quadratic speedup from QAE is theoretical; experiments run only on simulators and small toy problems.

experiments.description: Counterparty credit risk (PFE) experiment using a two-time-step, two-risk-factor quantum circuit with correlated normal returns, time aggregation, and IQAE on a simulator.

algorithm.variant: Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation (IQAE) for PFE/CDF estimation

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each marginal stock-return distribution is discretized with q qubits for each of N=2 time steps; distributions are added across time steps, then a comparator marks whether exposure is below a threshold for CDF estimation.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Estimate the CDF of exposure at t=1 and t=2 years and derive PFE quantiles.

problem_instance.description: Two-asset counterparty credit risk portfolio of bought call options on MSFT and AAPL, with zero strike so option PV equals stock price; initial collateral offsets initial exposure.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: Ten-day returns calibrated from historical data, then covariance scaled to annual horizon by factor 252/10

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Historical ten-day covariance matrix from market-risk section scaled to annual horizon; zero drifts assumed; two-year projection horizon discretized into two equidistant time steps; exposure quantiles computed at 90%, 95%, and 99%.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Quantum simulator results compared with closed-form classical exposure distributions; CDFs and quantiles reported for t=1 and t=2.

implementation_details.classical_solver: closed-form classical computation of exposure CDFs
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Calibration of correlated normal returns; annualization of covariance matrix; closed-form exposure distribution used as reference.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Quantile extraction from classical CDF; relative unsigned error computed against quantum estimates.

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical Monte Carlo-style sampling / closed-form classical exposure computation
speedup_claims.conditions: QAE / IQAE estimation of exposure CDFs
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper emphasizes that the practical setup still requires many qubits and that discretization error is significant for q=2; q=3 is more tolerable.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) convergence for QAE estimation error; quadratic improvement over Monte Carlo-style sampling

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not quantified; authors indicate realistic CCR problems require thousands of risk factors and many time steps
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Large-scale fault‑tolerant machines with orders-of-magnitude more qubits than current hardware
limiting_factors: Multi‑period stochastic processes dramatically increase qubit requirements
Ancilla qubits needed for addition and comparison circuits
Discretization errors from low qubit counts
Classical closed‑form solutions available for simple cases

notes: The paper states the computations are on a quantum simulator using Qiskit, but no specific backend/device is named.

The full total qubit count is not explicitly summarized as a single number; the paper gives q=2 or q=3 qubits per risk factor/time-step block plus ancillas, so total num_qubits is left null rather than inferred.
The paper presents simulator demonstrations only and explicitly notes practical applications are out of reach with current hardware.

experiments.description: Noise-sensitivity experiment applied to the counterparty credit risk circuit, using a simplified bit-flip noise model on a simulator to assess impact on exposure quantiles.

algorithm.variant: IQAE under a simplified bit-flip noise model

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Same exposure-CDF circuit as the CCR experiment, with noise injected into all one- and two-qubit gates and final measurement.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Quantify how noise perturbs the estimated exposure CDF and quantiles.

problem_instance.description: Counterparty credit risk exposure at t=1 year for the two-asset options portfolio from the main CCR example.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: Same as main CCR example; q=3 discretization per risk factor

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Same as main CCR example; noise study varies only the circuit noise level.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compare noisy vs noise-free CDFs and relative errors in typical PFE quantiles as noise level is scaled around 0.1% by powers of two.

implementation_details.classical_solver: noise-free simulator reference and classical CDF comparison
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Same calibration as main CCR example.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Relative error of noisy quantiles computed against noise-free simulator output.

results.unit: relative error in 90% PFE quantile at 0.1% noise

speedup_claims.conditions: IQAE under a simplified bit-flip noise model on all one- and two-qubit gates and final measurement
speedup_claims.caveats: Noise substantially degrades the estimates; the paper reports that even promising q=3 circuits become essentially unusable at typical noise levels.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(M^-1) convergence for QAE estimation error, degraded by noise

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not applicable; noise prevents useful results even for toy examples
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Fault‑tolerant error‑corrected quantum computers with drastically lower gate error rates
limiting_factors: Noise levels around 0.1% per gate produce >25% errors in risk estimates
No error mitigation or correction used
NISQ devices unsuitable for accurate financial risk estimation

notes: The paper explicitly states a simplified noise model on a quantum simulator, not a real device.
The noise section specifies q=3 qubits per risk factor and time point t=1, but does not restate a single total qubit count for the full noisy circuit; total num_qubits is therefore left null.
Section 6 shows that realistic noise levels make risk estimates unusable.
Authors conclude that current NISQ devices cannot support these applications.
